zone: Bridge Creek and North Fork — Mount Goode
_areas_note: Goode's uncovered routes are Megalodon Ridge and Northeast Face, both NE-side, which is what Bridge Creek serves; its Northeast Buttress and Southwest Couloir already carry camping and are skipped. The research flagged that the Bedayn Couloir and the SW side are approached from Park Creek out of Stehekin instead, so a future SW route must not inherit these camps.

sites.name: North Fork Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT junction
sites.capacity: Small designated hiker camp with a handful of numbered sites; the site is reserved by name on the permit
sites.water: Reliable year round — Bridge Creek and the North Fork run beside the camp
sites.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round; reserve the specific camp on Recreation.gov or take a walk-up from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee applies.
sites.notes: This sits right at the junction where the PCT leaves Bridge Creek for the North Fork, roughly ten miles in from the SR 20 trailhead, so it is the natural first-night stop for a party that started late. It is a long way below the climb, which means a very big second day to reach the glacier bivies. Its value is logistical rather than tactical — it shortens the drive-day push without needing a cross-country zone permit. Being a valley-bottom camp in forest, expect bugs through midsummer.

sites.name: Walker Park Camp
sites.capacity: Small designated camp, a couple of parties at most
sites.water: Reliable — sits on the North Fork of Bridge Creek
sites.permit: Designated-camp permit, booked by camp name; same NPS fee structure as any Bridge Creek camp, and it must be carried for the night you actually sleep there.
sites.notes: Roughly two miles up the North Fork trail from the junction, this is the first camp that meaningfully shortens the walk to the Goode Glacier drainage. The tread to here is still ordinary maintained trail, so it is an easy target even arriving in the dark. Parties usually treat it as a place to shed weight rather than a base, since the climb is still hours of rough ground above. No elevation is recorded — the valley section stays well under 4,000 ft, but no confident figure was sourced.

sites.name: Grizzly Creek Camp
sites.capacity: Larger than the other North Fork camps and open to stock parties, so you may be sharing it
sites.water: Reliable — Grizzly Creek and the North Fork are both at hand
sites.permit: Designated-camp permit reserved by name through Recreation.gov or issued walk-up at Marblemount; per-person and reservation fees apply.
sites.notes: About four miles up the North Fork trail, this is the last designated camp before the country turns unpleasant, and the practical decision point for the whole approach. Beyond it the tread gets brushy and faint — stinging nettles are a recurring complaint and long trousers are worth carrying regardless of the heat — and the North Fork has to be forded or crossed on a log, with difficulty that swings hard with snowmelt. A party arriving late, or facing high water, is usually better off sleeping here than committing to the bushwhack and the crossing in poor light.

sites.name: Fireweed Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT
sites.capacity: Designated camp with hiker and stock use
sites.permit: Designated-camp permit, same Recreation.gov / Marblemount walk-up system and the same per-person and reservation fees.
sites.notes: A Bridge Creek corridor camp on the PCT well short of the North Fork junction, near the Twisp Pass trail area. It is only useful to a Goode party as an overflow choice when the North Fork camps are booked out, which happens in peak season because so few sites serve this valley. Camping here adds miles to an already long approach day. Treat it as a fallback rather than a plan.

sites.name: Goode Glacier approach bivy, timbered knoll
sites.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small tents on a timbered knoll
sites.water: Meltwater from the Goode Glacier drainage nearby, but flow is seasonal and can be a walk away or thin late in the year
sites.permit: Inside the Goode CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE, not a designated camp — the permit is issued for the zone, party size is capped at six, no campfires, and camping is only allowed on durable ground such as snow, rock or bare earth.
sites.notes: Reached by leaving the North Fork trail after Grizzly Creek, fording the creek and grinding up timber and scree beside the drainage off the Goode Glacier, this is the classic first bivy under the buttress. Reports differ on whether it is the better choice: it sits noticeably west of the line of travel, so some parties consider the extra push to higher ground worth doing. Sparse timber gives a little shelter, which matters more here than the small elevation saving. Human waste goes in a cathole or is packed out above treeline, and there is no toilet.

sites.name: Upper bivy in the rock bands east of the buttress toe
sites.capacity: Tight — commonly described as just enough flat ground for a party of about four
sites.water: Running meltwater has been found at or near these sites, but it is snow-fed and not dependable once the drainage dries out later in the season
sites.permit: Goode cross-country zone permit, six-person maximum, no fires, durable surfaces only; zone camping must also keep clear of designated camps and trails by the park's stated distances.
sites.notes: Sitting in the rock bands just east of where the Northeast Buttress meets the ground, this puts you at the base with a few hundred feet already banked for summit day, which is the argument for grinding past the lower knoll. The exact elevation is reported inconsistently — figures in the 5,400 to 5,600 ft range all refer to broadly the same shelf system, so navigate to the terrain rather than to a number. It is exposed and rocky, so a poor choice in unsettled weather compared with the timbered ground lower down. Confirm you have water before committing to it late in the summer.
